title: CQ
full_review:
A young American filmmaker in Paris gets a chance to make his mark by directing a low-budget sci-fi flick in the quirky but flat "CQ" (MGM).

Director Roman Coppola, son of Francis Ford Coppola, makes his directorial debut in "CQ" much like Paul (Jeremy Davies), the low-key American filmmaker in 1969 Paris does in Coppola's film. While editing "Dragonfly," a "Barbarella"-like sci-fi actioner, Paul is asked to take over the project when the temperamental director, Andrzej (Gerard Depardieu), can't find an ending for the movie. Andrzej's judgment has also been clouded by his infatuation with the film's star, Valentine (Angela Lindvall), who plays Dragonfly, the kittenish secret agent dressed in skin-tight pink leather. So, the demanding Italian producer Enzo (an excellent Giancarlo Giannini) fires Andrzej and hires Paul.

Though Paul tries hard to make "Dragonfly" work, he remains more concerned with his own project, which he believes shows the truth in cinema. A collection of shots of coffee mugs, tea kettles, his pouty French girlfriend Marlene (Elodie Bouchez) in various states of undress and, finally, long rambling lectures made by Paul from his throne on the toilet comprise his supposedly edgy black-and-white piece. Paul's personal work might be interpreted as a pointed jab by Coppola at the pretensions of cinema and filmmakers, but instead it never gets off the ground.

This movie-within-a-movie is Coppola's tribute to the passion for cinema that was so fervent in Europe during the 1960s. But despite the eventful narrative and the Paris and Rome settings, the film remains grounded with uninspired characterizations. Paul, who takes the art of cinema very seriously and is obsessed with making an honest film about his own life -- no matter how boring it may turn out to be -- is a dullard. Throughout the film he wears the same world-weary expression behind his shaggy hair and black suit, white shirt and thin black tie. Depardieu spices things up during the limited screen time he has, but can't lift the film entirely. And Jason Schwartzman makes an even briefer appearance as an eccentric and talentless director whom Enzo hires before committing to Paul. However, Schwartzman is flamboyant and fun, adding a little pizzazz to an otherwise drab story.

Coppola, who wrote the screenplay as well, has trouble bringing all the loose ends together coherently. At various points it seems as if several different subplots may come together to form an interesting point or revelation. But this never happens.

"CQ" alternately pokes fun at or reveres the cinema of the intoxicating days of the 1960s, but when everything is pieced together, it doesn't create enough momentum to transport the viewer.

Due to frontal nudity, a sexual encounter and brief rough language and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted
